title: A method for any LLD problem
idea: A repeatable LLD method turns a vague prompt into classes in fixed steps: clarify use cases, find entities, assign behaviour, connect them, code the core, then extend.

analogy.text: Staging a play: agree the plot, cast the roles, give each role its lines, decide who speaks to whom, rehearse one scene, then adapt.
analogy.breaks: Actors improvise when lost; a class does only what its contract says.

points: Clarify first: list use cases, rules and limits; agree what is out of scope.
Nouns in use cases become candidate classes; verbs become methods on the data owner.
Put an interface only where the prompt or interviewer hints that behaviour will vary.
Code one use case end to end, then walk a failure case through it.

hero.title: Bike-share docks through the six steps

steps.caption: Clarify: riders unlock bikes and dock them at any station; a bike has one rider; riders have a ride limit.
Entities: Bike, Station, Rider and Ride. A ride is a noun too, and it records who has which bike.
Behaviour: add a `BikeShare` service that owns bikes, docks and active rides; `unlock` and `dock` go there.
Relations: a Ride has-a Rider and has-a Bike. The limit may vary, so it becomes `RideLimit`.
Code the unlock path first, then walk a failure through it: a stranger docking someone else's bike.
Follow-up: family accounts may ride two bikes at once. Find the step this change belongs to.
It lands in Relations: `Rider` gains a family flag and a new `RideLimit` lambda reads it. `BikeShare` stays untouched.

code.title: Skipping the method
code.caption: Straight to code with two maps. No Ride entity, so nobody knows who has a bike.

walk.text: State is two loose maps of strings. The relationship between rider and bike is missing.
Unlock looks fine: it blocks a bike that is out and counts the ride.
Dock trusts the caller. It cannot check the rider, because no record says who unlocked.
Bob docks Alice's bike, then a bike that was never unlocked. Both succeed.
Alice still counts a ride, Bob's count goes negative, and B9 now exists.

code.title: Following the method
code.caption: Each step of the method is visible: entities as records, a limit contract, one owning service.

walk.text: Step 2 as code: immutable records. `Ride` is the noun the rushed version missed.
The varying rule is a one-method interface; failures share one unchecked exception type.
`BikeShare` owns bikes, docks and rides, so the verbs live here. The limit arrives by constructor.
`unlock` checks the bike exists, is docked and the rider is under the limit, then records a ride.
`dock` refuses anyone who is not the recorded rider, then docks the bike at any station.
The limit rule is a lambda. The family two-bike limit lives here, not inside `BikeShare`.
Bob's dock and Alice's second unlock are refused; B1 ends up docked at Park.

pitfalls: Coding before listing use cases; you discover a missing entity, like Ride, after the bugs.
Turning every noun into a class; attributes such as colour or station name belong inside one.
Adding interfaces everywhere up front; the interviewer sees ceremony instead of design judgement.

quiz.q: The interviewer adds: rides over 30 minutes cost extra. Where does it fit best?
options: A start time on Ride, and a FarePolicy contract
A fare field on Rider, updated by every method
A static helper class called from main
A new subclass of Bike for long rides
quiz.why: Ride length is a fact about one ride, so the start time lives on `Ride`. Fare rules vary, so they sit behind a contract like `RideLimit`.

takeaway: Clarify, find nouns, assign verbs, connect, code one path, then extend.

starters: How do I decide whether a noun is a class or just a field?
How many use cases should I clarify before starting to code?
What should I do if I realise mid-interview that I missed an entity?
